diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_MISSING_OUTPUT
diagnostics.message: no output file given; use -o FILE or --output FILE
diagnostics.cause: The output file name is a mandatory parameter, so that the compiler never guesses where to put the generated binary and never overwrites a file the caller did not name.  Add -o followed by the path of the executable to create.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_NO_INPUT
diagnostics.message: no input files given
diagnostics.cause: At least one source file must be named on the command line.  This usually means the file list was produced by a shell glob that matched nothing, or that every argument was consumed as the value of an option.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_BAD_SUFFIX
diagnostics.message: input file '{path}' does not have the '.pl4g' suffix
diagnostics.cause: Source files are recognized by their '.pl4g' suffix.  A file with any other suffix is rejected rather than guessed at, because silently treating an unrelated file as source would produce a cascade of confusing syntax errors.  Rename the file, or check whether an option value was mistaken for a positional argument.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_OPTION
diagnostics.message: unrecognized command line option '{option}'
diagnostics.cause: The option is not known to this compiler.  Both compiler implementations accept the same options, so an option that works with one and not the other is a defect worth reporting.  Use --help to list the accepted options.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_DUPLICATE_OUTPUT
diagnostics.message: output file specified more than once; previously '{previous}'
diagnostics.cause: Exactly one output file may be named.  Repeating -o is rejected rather than resolved by taking the last one, because a generated command line that accumulates an extra -o is far more likely to be a defect in the generator than a deliberate override.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_NOT_IMPLEMENTED
diagnostics.message: option '{option}' is accepted by this compiler but not yet implemented
diagnostics.cause: The bootstrap compiler accepts the full option set of the final compiler so that build systems need not distinguish between them, but it does not implement every option yet.  This is a limitation of the bootstrap compiler, not an error in the command line.

spec.requirement: The Python implementation will accept the same parameters as the actual, full compiler.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_MISSING_ARGUMENT
diagnostics.message: option '{option}' requires an argument
diagnostics.cause: The option takes a value which was not supplied, usually because it was the last word of the command line or because the following word began with a dash and was taken as a separate option.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_BAD_ARGUMENT
diagnostics.message: invalid argument '{value}' for option '{option}'; expected one of {expected}
diagnostics.cause: The option accepts only a fixed set of values.  Check the spelling of the value against the list in the message or in --help.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_TARGET
diagnostics.message: unknown target '{triple}'
diagnostics.cause: No backend is registered for this target triple.  The bootstrap compiler supports a subset of the targets the final compiler will support; the supported ones are listed by --help.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_WARNING
diagnostics.message: unknown warning name '{name}' in '{option}'
diagnostics.cause: The name given to -W or -Wno- does not match any controllable diagnostic.  The controllable names are the 'option' fields of the shared diagnostic catalog; note that errors cannot be disabled.

spec.requirement: Errors and warnings the compiler emits can be handled in the code.  To enable this, errors and warnings must be unique, constant, and consistent numbers.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_INPUT_UNREADABLE
diagnostics.message: cannot read '{path}': {reason}
diagnostics.cause: The source file could not be opened or read.  Common causes are a mistyped path, a file that was removed between the glob and the compilation, or insufficient permissions.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_OUTPUT_UNWRITABLE
diagnostics.message: cannot write '{path}': {reason}
diagnostics.cause: The output file could not be created or written.  Common causes are a non-existent directory, insufficient permissions, or a full file system.  The compiler writes the output only after code generation has succeeded, so a failure here leaves any previous output untouched.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INVALID_UTF8
diagnostics.message: source file is not valid UTF-8 (at byte offset {offset})

args.name: offset
args.description: byte offset of the first invalid sequence

diagnostics.cause: Source text must be encoded in UTF-8.  A file saved in a single-byte encoding such as ISO-8859-1 will fail here as soon as it contains a non-ASCII character.  Re-encode the file as UTF-8.

spec.requirement: The compiler and well as any generated program requires that the encoding of text uses UTF-8 encoding.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNEXPECTED_CHAR
diagnostics.message: unexpected character {char} in source

args.name: char
args.description: the character and its code point

diagnostics.cause: The character cannot begin any token.  Since the language uses Unicode glyphs for several operators, this is often a glyph that resembles the intended one without being it, such as a hyphen-minus where a dash was meant, or a full-width character pasted from another document.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNTERMINATED_STRING
diagnostics.message: unterminated string literal
diagnostics.cause: A string literal was not closed before the end of the line.  String literals do not span lines; a closing quotation mark may be missing, or a backslash immediately before it may have escaped it unintentionally.

spec.requirement: Strings are written as in C/C++ and many other languages enclosed in `"` and supporting an escape notation like modern C and C++ for special characters as well as the Unicode notation.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_BAD_ESCAPE
diagnostics.message: unknown escape sequence '\\{char}' in string literal
diagnostics.cause: The character following the backslash does not form a recognized escape sequence.  The recognized escapes follow modern C and C++, including the \\u and \\U Unicode notations.  A literal backslash must be written as two backslashes.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_ASCII_SUBSTITUTE
diagnostics.message: '{ascii}' is accepted as a substitute for '{glyph}'
diagnostics.cause: The language is meant to be generated rather than typed, so the Unicode glyph is the canonical spelling and is what the compiler itself emits.  Multi-character ASCII substitutes are accepted for convenience while editing by hand; single characters are never substitutes, so that they remain available for future language features.  The substitution is reported only when this warning is asked for, since it is accepted usage rather than a defect.

spec.requirement: It is not important that keyboard support for entering the language exists which opens the door to using Unicode glyphs for operators and functions.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INTEGER_RANGE
diagnostics.message: integer literal {literal} does not fit in type '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: The value of the literal lies outside the range the type can represent.  Because the language admits no undefined behaviour and no surprising interpretation of inputs, an out-of-range literal is an error rather than a silent truncation or wrap-around.

spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_BAD_LITERAL_SUFFIX
diagnostics.message: '{suffix}' is not an integer type, so it cannot be the suffix of a literal
diagnostics.cause: The suffix of an integer literal is the name of the integer type the literal has: one of i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32 and u64.  Any other name, including the name of a type that is not an integer, has no meaning there.

spec.requirement: An integer literal states its type with a suffix naming that type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_LONELY_NEGATIVE
diagnostics.message: the sign of a negative literal must be followed immediately by digits
diagnostics.cause: A leading superscript minus is part of how a number is written, not an operator applied to one, so nothing may stand between it and the digits -- no space, and no other expression.  Writing it apart from the digits would make it a second spelling of subtraction, which is what having a separate glyph for the sign avoids.

spec.requirement: A negative literal is written with a leading superscript minus and no space: nothing stands between the sign and the digits.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INCONSISTENT_INDENT
diagnostics.message: indentation does not match any enclosing block
diagnostics.cause: A line is indented less than the current block but more than the block that encloses it, so it belongs to neither.  This usually results from mixing tab and space indentation, or from a generator that computed an indentation width inconsistently.

spec.requirement: Layout-based syntax uses rules and syntax similar to Python.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_MIXED_BLOCK_STYLE
diagnostics.message: layout and explicit '{{' '}}' block syntax cannot be mixed within one block
diagnostics.cause: A single block uses one notation throughout: either indentation, or braces with semicolon-separated statements.  Nested blocks may each choose their own notation, but a block may not change notation part way through.

spec.requirement: Indentation and explicit syntax cannot be mixed for individual blocks but properly nested blocks can have different syntaxes.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_TAB_INDENT
diagnostics.message: tab character used for indentation
diagnostics.cause: Indentation is measured in characters, so a tab would make the layout depend on a tab width that is not part of the language.  Because the language admits no surprising interpretation of inputs, tabs are rejected in indentation rather than assigned an arbitrary width.

spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN
diagnostics.message: expected {expected}, found {found}
diagnostics.cause: The parser reached a token that cannot continue the construct being parsed.  The message names what would have been accepted at that point.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_EXPECTED_BLOCK
diagnostics.message: expected ':' or '{{' to begin the function body
diagnostics.cause: A function header is followed either by a colon and an indented block, or by a brace-enclosed block of semicolon-separated statements.  A header with neither has no body.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: In layout format, the function header is followed by a colon, a newline, and then the properly indented code.  When the function header is followed by a `{` it uses the explicit syntax and continues until the respective closing `}`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FILESTRUCT_UNEXPECTED_TOPLEVEL
diagnostics.message: {construct} is not allowed at the top level of a file
diagnostics.cause: Only module handling, compile-time assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions and function definitions may appear at the top level.  Statements that execute at run time belong inside a function; use a constructor function if the intent was to run code before the startup function.

spec.requirement: At the top level of a file one can find: module handling, compile-time expressions as assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions, function definitions

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_DUPLICATE_PARAMETER
diagnostics.message: parameter '{name}' is declared more than once
diagnostics.cause: Each parameter of a function must have a distinct name, since otherwise a reference to that name in the body would be ambiguous.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: fn NAME(ARG1: TYPE1, [ARGN: TYPEN]) → RETVALTYPE BLOCK

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_EXPECTED_COLON
diagnostics.message: expected ':' after the name of the variable
diagnostics.cause: A variable definition always carries a colon, whether or not the type is written after it: `let x: u8 = 3u8` states the type, and `let x := 3u8` leaves it to be taken from the value.  The colon is what marks the construct as a definition.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_MISSING_INITIALIZER
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is defined without a value
diagnostics.cause: A variable is given its value where it is defined; there is no form that leaves one uninitialized.  A variable that had no value would have to hold something the program never named, which is exactly the kind of unstated meaning this language does not admit -- and no rule about what that something is would make it stated.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_PAREN
diagnostics.message: expected ')' to close the group
diagnostics.cause: Parentheses in an expression say which operator applies to what, so one that is opened has to be closed.  Check for a missing operand or an operator written where an operand was wanted.

spec.requirement: An expression may be enclosed in parentheses, which say how its operators group and mean nothing else.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_MEMBER
diagnostics.message: expected the name of something after '.'
diagnostics.cause: A dot names something through the thing it belongs to, so a name has to follow it.  Nothing else may.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_EXPECTED_NAME
diagnostics.message: expected the name of a module, written as a string
diagnostics.cause: What `import` is given is the name of a module, written in quotes.  It is not an expression and is not computed: the module is found and read while the program is being compiled, so the name has to be there to read.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_QUALIFIED
diagnostics.message: '{name}' names a module, which cannot be given a type or made mutable

args.name: name
args.description: the name the module is bound to

diagnostics.cause: A module is not a value.  Nothing can be computed from one, nothing of it survives into the program but the definitions it holds, and there is accordingly nothing to give a type to and nothing to change.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_INSIDE_FUNCTION
diagnostics.message: '{name}' imports a module inside a function, where a module cannot go

args.name: name
args.description: the name the module was to be bound to

diagnostics.cause: A module is read while the program is being compiled and what it holds belongs to the program, not to one function that happens to run.  An import therefore stands at the top level of a file, where the things it brings in are things the file has.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, at the top level of that file.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_NOT_ASSOCIATIVE
diagnostics.message: '{first}' and '{second}' cannot be written one after the other
diagnostics.cause: Some operators join two things and no more, because a third would have two readings and neither is what anyone means.  A comparison answers with a truth value, so `a < b < c` would compare that answer with a number.  ⊼ and ⊽ are not associative at all: `a ⊼ b ⊼ c` is one thing grouped to the left and a different thing grouped to the right.  Where one of those really was meant, parentheses say which; where a value was meant to lie between two others, that is two comparisons joined with ∧.

spec.requirement: The six comparisons share one level of precedence and do not associate, and neither do ⊼ and ⊽.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_EXPECTED_EQUALS
diagnostics.message: a type definition is written 'type NAME = ...'
diagnostics.cause: The name of the type is followed by `=` and then by what the type is made of.  There is no form that declares a name without saying what it stands for: a type whose parts are not written is a type nothing can be said about, and the language has no forward declarations because it reads every definition of a file before it checks any of them.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A type definition is written `type NAME = ...`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_EXPECTED_COLON
diagnostics.message: each part of a type is written 'NAME : TYPE'
diagnostics.cause: A field of a product and a variant of a sum are both written as a name, a colon and a type -- the same shape a parameter and a variable are written with, so that one habit serves for all of them.  A part with no name would be one that could only be reached by counting, and the specification lets the compiler reorder a product's fields, so counting is exactly what it must not be possible to do.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: Each part of a type definition is written `NAME : TYPE`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_MIXED_SEPARATORS
diagnostics.message: this definition separates its parts with {found} after separating them with {first}

args.name: first
args.description: the separator the definition started with

diagnostics.cause: The separator is what says which kind of type is being defined: `;` for a product, which holds all of its parts at once, and `|` for a sum, which holds exactly one of them.  A definition using both would be saying two things about itself, and there is no type that is both.  Which one was meant is what to decide; the first separator is where the definition said so.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: One type definition uses one separator throughout.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_FIRST_SEPARATOR
diagnostics.message: the definition separated its parts with this
diagnostics.cause: Attached to the report of a definition that changed separator part way, pointing at the one it began with.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: One type definition uses one separator throughout.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_NO_PARTS
diagnostics.message: a type with no parts is 'void' written at greater length
diagnostics.cause: A product of no fields holds nothing, and a sum of no variants has no value at all; `void` is the type of what carries no information, and the language admits one spelling per meaning.  Where a type is wanted that is a name for another type, that is what the to-do list calls an alias and the language does not have yet.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A type definition has at least one part.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_EXPECTED_ARMS
diagnostics.message: the arms of a 'match' follow it, indented or in braces
diagnostics.cause: `match` takes a value apart, so it is written with the value and then the arms that take its alternatives: a colon and an indented run of them, or a braced one.  There is no form with no arms, because a `match` that takes nothing apart does nothing.

spec.requirement: A `match` is written with its arms in one of the two block notations.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_EXPECTED_VALUES
diagnostics.message: the values of an enumeration follow it, indented or in braces
diagnostics.cause: `enum NAME` says what the type is called and nothing about what it holds, so the names of its values follow: a colon and an indented run of them, or a braced one.  Where a type was named as well, the colon that opens the block is a second one -- the first belongs to the type.

spec.requirement: An enumeration is written with its values in one of the two block notations.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_NO_VALUES
diagnostics.message: an enumeration with no values is a type nothing can have
diagnostics.cause: Every value of an enumeration is one of the names its definition lists, so a definition that lists none describes a type no value can be of.  `void` is the type of what carries no information, and is what a program that wants one should say.

spec.requirement: An enumeration has at least one value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_EXPECTED_VALUE
diagnostics.message: a value of an enumeration is given a number or another of its names, not {found}
diagnostics.cause: `NAME = 4` says which number the value is stored as; `NAME = other` says it is the one `other` already stands for, which is how two names are given one value on purpose.  Nothing else may follow the `=`: an enumeration's values are known while the program is compiled, so there is nothing for an expression to be worked out from.

spec.requirement: A value of an enumeration is given a number or the name of an earlier one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: unknown attribute '{name}'
diagnostics.cause: The attribute name is not one the compiler knows.  Attribute names are not an open namespace: an unrecognized name is an error rather than an ignored annotation, so that a misspelling can never silently drop a property the code depends on.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_DUPLICATE
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' is applied more than once to the same object
diagnostics.cause: An attribute may appear only once per object.  Where an attribute admits several variants, the variant is selected by a parameter rather than by repeating the attribute.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_BAD_ARGUMENTS
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' {problem}
diagnostics.cause: The arguments do not match the attribute's declared signature.  Attributes take positional arguments first and named arguments after, in the manner of a function call.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_NOT_APPLICABLE
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' cannot be applied to {target}

args.name: target
args.description: the kind of object it was applied to

diagnostics.cause: Each attribute declares the kinds of object it may annotate.  The startup, constructor, destructor and test attributes, for instance, describe how a function participates in program execution and are meaningless on a type or a variable.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_CONFLICT
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' conflicts with '{other}' on the same object
diagnostics.cause: The two attributes request incompatible treatment.  A function cannot, for example, be both the startup function and a destructor, since the two describe different points in the program's life.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_EXPECT_NOT_RAISED
diagnostics.message: no diagnostic {number} was raised here, though one was expected
diagnostics.cause: `expect` asserts that the construct raises the diagnostic, so an expectation nothing meets is a statement about the program that is not true.  It is an error rather than a warning because the attribute exists to be relied upon: a reader takes it as saying what the construct does, and a stale one says something false while hiding nothing.  Where the intent is only to keep a diagnostic quiet, whether or not it arises, that is what `@[ignore(NUMBER)]` is for.

spec.requirement: `@[ignore(NUMBER)]` keeps the diagnostic with that number from being reported.  `@[expect(NUMBER)]` does the same and is an error where the diagnostic is not raised.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_EXPECT_UNKNOWN_NUMBER
diagnostics.message: {number} is not the number of any diagnostic
diagnostics.cause: The number must be one the compiler can emit.  They are four digits, they are the same in every implementation, and the definitive list of them is the shared catalog; a number that is not in it can never be raised, so naming it could only ever be a mistake.

spec.requirement: `@[ignore(NUMBER)]` keeps the diagnostic with that number from being reported.  `@[expect(NUMBER)]` does the same and is an error where the diagnostic is not raised.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_SEPARATE_LISTS
diagnostics.message: attributes attached to one thing are written as one list, not {count}
diagnostics.cause: Two lists attached to one definition say exactly what one list holding both would say, so there would be two ways to write one thing and a reader would have to know both.  Write `@[one, two]` rather than `@[one]` followed by `@[two]`.  A blank line between them makes no difference: it changes nothing about what they attach to.

spec.requirement: Several attributes may be given in one list, and one list precedes a definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_EMPTY_ARGUMENTS
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' takes no arguments here, so it is written without parentheses
diagnostics.cause: An empty argument list says exactly what no argument list says, so there would be two ways to write one thing.  Write `@[inline]` rather than `@[inline()]`.  The parentheses are how an attribute carries arguments, and an attribute carrying none does not need them.

spec.requirement: Several attributes may be given in one list, and one list precedes a definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FILESTRUCT_DUPLICATE_DEFINITION
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is defined more than once
diagnostics.cause: Two definitions at the top level share a name.  Since compilation covers the whole program at once, this also catches a name defined in two different source files.

spec.requirement: At the top level of a file one can find: module handling, compile-time expressions as assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions, function definitions

diagnostics.name: LANG_FILESTRUCT_PREVIOUS_DEFINITION
diagnostics.message: '{name}' was previously defined here
diagnostics.cause: Attached to the report of a duplicate definition, to point at the one that was seen first.

spec.requirement: At the top level of a file one can find: module handling, compile-time expressions as assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions, function definitions

diagnostics.name: LANG_FILESTRUCT_UNDEFINED_NAME
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not defined
diagnostics.cause: No definition of this name is visible.  Definitions need not appear before their use, because the grammar is context-free and the compiler collects every top-level definition before checking any function body; so this really means no definition exists anywhere in the program.

spec.requirement: Operations of the compiler must be parallelizable and to ensure this the grammar has to be context-free

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_NOT_MUTABLE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' cannot be changed; it was not defined with 'mut'
diagnostics.cause: A variable can be assigned to only where its definition says so.  The default is the one that cannot change, because a name that keeps its value is easier to reason about and is what the language's functional style calls for; saying 'mut' is how a program states that this one does not.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable can be changed only if it was defined with `mut`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_DEFINED_HERE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is defined here
diagnostics.cause: Attached to the report of an assignment to a variable that cannot change, to point at the definition that would have to say 'mut'.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable can be changed only if it was defined with `mut`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_VALUE_UNUSED
diagnostics.message: the value given to '{name}' here is never read
diagnostics.cause: Nothing reads the value between the point it is given and the point it is replaced or the variable goes out of scope, so giving it cannot affect what the program does.  Either the value was meant to be used and something reads the wrong thing, or it was not and the line can go.  Where it is deliberate -- a program written to exercise the compiler, say -- say so with `@[expect(4006)]`.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_TOPLEVEL_UNREAD
diagnostics.message: the program writes '{name}' and never reads it

args.name: name
args.description: the variable at the top level

diagnostics.cause: The program writes this variable and never reads it back, so what is written cannot affect what the program does.  This is the rule that catches an unread value inside a function, asked of a variable at the top level; because a variable there can be named from anywhere in the program, it is a question about the whole program rather than about the scope that defines it, and it is answered once every function has been checked.  Either something was meant to read it and reads the wrong thing, or the variable and the writes to it can go.  A variable the program exports is never reported, since something outside may read it.  Where it is deliberate -- a program written to exercise the compiler, say -- say so with `@[expect(4007)]` on the definition.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

The extension is added where the name does not already have it.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.  Only what the module exports can be named.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.  Only what the module exports can be named.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: unknown type '{name}'
diagnostics.cause: No type of this name is in scope.  The built-in types are i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f32, f64, bool and void.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_RETURN_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: returning '{found}' from a function declared to return '{expected}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the returned expression

diagnostics.cause: The type of the returned expression differs from the function's declared return type, and the language performs no implicit conversion that would hide the difference.  Either change the declared return type or convert the value explicitly.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_INITIALIZER_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: initializing '{name}', which is of type '{expected}', with a value of type '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: The value a variable is given must have the variable's type; the language performs no conversion that would hide a difference between them.  Either change the declared type, leave it out so that it is taken from the value, or convert the value explicitly.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_ASSIGNMENT_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: assigning a value of type '{found}' to '{name}', which is of type '{expected}'
diagnostics.cause: A variable keeps the type it was defined with, and the value assigned to it must have that type; the language performs no conversion that would hide a difference between them.

spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_OPERAND_NOT_INTEGER
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' is defined on integers, not on '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: The bitwise operators work on the bits of an integer, and nothing else has bits to work on.  A truth value is not a one-bit integer here: `bool` has two values and no representation the language promises, so `&` on one has nothing to mean.  Use the logical operators for truth values.

spec.requirement: The bitwise operators are defined on integer values only.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_OPERAND_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: the operands of '{operator}' are of different types, '{expected}' and '{found}'

args.name: expected
args.description: the type of the left operand

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the right operand

diagnostics.cause: An operator applies to two values of one type and gives a value of that type.  Nothing is widened to make two types meet: a value of one width becoming a value of another is exactly the kind of quiet reinterpretation this language does not admit.  Give the narrower operand the wider type outright.

spec.requirement: Both sides of an operator have the same type, and the result has it too.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_OPERAND_NOT_COMPARABLE
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' compares numbers and truth values, not '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: Equality is defined on the types whose values can be told apart one from another -- numbers, truth values, and in time strings.  It is not defined on a type whose values have no such notion, and answering such a comparison with anything would be inventing an answer.  Ordering is narrower still and is defined on numbers alone, which is a different diagnostic.

spec.requirement: Exact comparisons are defined for numbers, truth values and strings.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_OPERAND_NOT_BOOLEAN
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' is defined on truth values, not on '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: The logical operators join truth values, and a number is not one.  There is no rule here that a number other than zero counts as true: C has that rule and it is where `if (x = 0)` and a good deal else comes from, and the bitwise operators are what applies to the bits of a number.  Where the question is whether a number is zero, `≠` asks it.

spec.requirement: The logical operators work on truth values only.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_NOTHING_IS_NOT_WRITTEN
diagnostics.message: a function that answers with nothing is written without the arrow
diagnostics.cause: There is one way to say that a function answers with nothing, and it is to say nothing: `fn prepare():` rather than `fn prepare() → void:`.  Writing it out would be a second spelling of the same thing, which the language admits nowhere -- and `void` is not a type a value can have, so naming it as one says less than leaving it out.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A function that answers with nothing is written without the arrow and without a type after it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_NOT_A_FUNCTION
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a function
diagnostics.cause: Only a function can be called.  A variable holds a value and a module is a place names are found in; neither is something to hand arguments to.  A call through a value that happens to be the address of a function will be a different thing, written differently, when there are addresses to hold.

spec.requirement: A function is called by writing its arguments after its name.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_WRONG_ARGUMENT_COUNT
diagnostics.message: '{name}' takes {expected} arguments, not {found}
diagnostics.cause: A call hands over exactly the arguments the function takes.  There are no defaults and nothing is variadic, so a count that does not match is a mistake and not a form of the call.

spec.requirement: A call hands over exactly the arguments the function takes, in order.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_HAS_NO_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' answers with nothing, so there is no value here to use
diagnostics.cause: A function whose header has no arrow answers with nothing, so a call to it has no answer: it cannot start a variable, be assigned, or be an operand.  The one place such a call may be written is where nothing is wanted of it -- as a statement of its own, or after `return` in a function that also answers with nothing, which is the call followed by returning and carries no value either.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A call to a function that answers with nothing has no answer, so naming one where a value is wanted is an error.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_ARGUMENT_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: argument {position} of '{name}' is '{expected}', not '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was written

diagnostics.cause: An argument has the type of the parameter it is handed to, and nothing is widened to make two types meet -- the same rule every other place a value is written into something follows.  A literal without a suffix takes the parameter's type, which is what lets a call be written with plain numbers.

spec.requirement: A call hands over exactly the arguments the function takes, in order.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_ANSWER_DOES_NOT_FIT
diagnostics.message: the answer to this is {value}, which does not fit '{type}'

args.name: type
args.description: the type it had to fit

diagnostics.cause: The operation faults when it runs, and both sides are known here, so it faults every time the program runs.  A program that must stop whenever it is started is one that need not be built, and saying so while it is being compiled costs nothing and is found without running anything.  Where going past the end is what was meant, the saturating operators are what say so.

spec.requirement: Where an overflow can be shown at compile time it is a compilation error rather than a fault.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_DIVISION_BY_ZERO
diagnostics.message: this divides by zero, so it never has an answer
diagnostics.cause: Dividing by zero has no answer, and a division answers with a result -- so this is well formed and its value is the error.  It is still almost certainly a mistake: the divisor is written down and is zero, so the error branch is the only one this program ever takes.  Where it is meant, `@[ignore(4215)]` says so.

spec.requirement: A division by a divisor written as zero is diagnosed.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_ROTATE_IS_UNSIGNED
diagnostics.message: a rotation turns the bits of an unsigned number, not of '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was rotated

diagnostics.cause: Turning bits round says nothing about a number that has a sign: the bit that would come round into the top is the one that says which sign it has, so the answer is a number unrelated to the one that went in.  A type says what a value *is* here, and a signed type says the value is a number.  Where the bits are what is wanted, an unsigned type is what says so.

spec.requirement: A rotation is defined on unsigned integers.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_EXACT_FLOAT_COMPARISON
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' on '{type}' asks whether two values are the one value
diagnostics.cause: A floating-point value is an approximation of the number it stands for, and two approximations arrived at by different routes are rarely the same approximation even where the numbers are the same.  So asking whether two of them are equal is nearly always asking the wrong question, and the answer is nearly always no.  The approximate comparisons `≅` and `≇` ask whether the two are within the tolerance of each other, which is the question that was usually meant.  Where the exact question is the one meant -- comparing a value against one it was assigned from, or against a number that every format holds exactly -- `@[ignore(4217)]` says so.

spec.requirement: An exact comparison of floating-point values is diagnosed.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_APPROXIMATE_NEEDS_A_FLOAT
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' compares floating-point values, not '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: The approximate comparisons exist because a floating-point value is an approximation, and two of them arrived at by different routes are rarely the one value.  An integer is not an approximation of anything: two integers are equal or they are not, and there is no error in one for a tolerance to allow for.  A truth value is not ordered at all.  So these six ask a question that only a floating-point type has, and the exact comparisons are what every other type is compared with.

spec.requirement: The approximate comparisons are defined on floating-point values only.

diagnostics.name: LANG_NAME_IS_THE_COMPILERS
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is a name the compiler provides and cannot be defined
diagnostics.cause: A name beginning with ⎕ belongs to the compiler.  A program may read and assign the ones that exist -- `⎕tolerance` is the only one so far -- and may not define one, which is what keeps the compiler free to add another without taking a name away from a program that was written before it existed.  APL marks its own system names with the same glyph for the same reason.  A name of your own is written without it.

spec.section: The Language / Names the compiler provides
spec.requirement: A name beginning with ⎕ may not be defined by a program.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_NOT_A_RESULT
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' takes a result, not '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what it was applied to

diagnostics.cause: `?` and `??` exist to get at the answer inside a result, which is a value that may not have one.  A value that is not a result has its answer and nothing else: there is nothing for either operator to take out of it and no other case for them to handle.  Where the value came from a division, it is a result and this is not it; everywhere else the operator can simply be left off.

spec.requirement: `?` and `??` apply to a value of a result type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_TRY_NEEDS_A_RESULT
diagnostics.message: '?' leaves the function with an error, and this one answers with '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: what the enclosing function answers with

diagnostics.cause: `?` hands the answer back where there is one and leaves the function carrying the error where there is not, so the function has to be one that can carry an error -- its own type must be a result whose error type is the same.  Where the function should not fail, `??` gives a value to use instead; where it should, say so in its type.

spec.requirement: `?` requires the enclosing function to answer with a result whose error type is the same.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_RESULT_OF_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: 'void?' is not a type: there is no answer for it to hold
diagnostics.cause: A result is an answer or the fact that there is none, and `void` is the type of what carries no information.  A result of it would be a truth value written as though it were something more, which is the kind of second spelling this language does not admit.  A function that either works or does not, and answers with nothing when it works, says so by answering with `bool` -- or, once an error carries a value, with that.

spec.requirement: The answer type of a result may not be `void`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_DIVISION_DOES_NOT_FIT
diagnostics.message: the answer to this would be {value}, which does not fit '{type}', so it never has one

args.name: type
args.description: the type it does not fit

diagnostics.cause: The most negative number of a signed type divided by minus one has a quotient one past the largest that type holds.  It is the only pair of operands other than a zero divisor that a division has no answer for.  A division answers with a result, so this is well formed and its value is the error -- but both operands are written down here, so the error is the only thing this program will get out of it.  `@[ignore(4223)]` says it is meant.

spec.requirement: A division written with operands that cannot have an answer is diagnosed.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_SPECIAL_NO_STARTUP
diagnostics.message: no function is marked as the startup function
diagnostics.cause: Every program needs the one function control is transferred to once the startup phase completes, and the specification states that compilation fails when none is marked.  Apply the startup attribute to the entry point.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Exactly one function can be marked this way.  If no function is marked as such compilation fails.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_SPECIAL_MULTIPLE_STARTUP
diagnostics.message: more than one function is marked as the startup function
diagnostics.cause: Exactly one function may carry the startup attribute, because control is transferred to a single entry point.  This commonly happens when two source files each define a startup function, or when a generator emitted the attribute on more than one candidate.  If both entry points really are needed, make one of them a constructor.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Exactly one function can be marked this way.  If no function is marked as such compilation fails.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_SPECIAL_PREVIOUS_STARTUP
diagnostics.message: the startup function '{name}' was marked here
diagnostics.cause: Attached to the report of a duplicate startup function, to point at the one that was seen first.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Exactly one function can be marked this way.  If no function is marked as such compilation fails.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_SPECIAL_BAD_SIGNATURE
diagnostics.message: the startup function must have the signature 'fn NAME() → {type}', but '{name}' {problem}

args.name: type
args.description: the type a startup function must return

diagnostics.cause: Control is transferred to the startup function without arguments, and the value it returns becomes the exit status of the process.  A signature with parameters would leave the arguments undefined.  The return type is the width of an exit status and nothing wider: what a program passes to the system is truncated to eight bits before anything can observe it, so a wider type would let a program state a status that cannot arrive.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: The startup function takes no parameters and returns `u8`, the width of an exit status.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_SPECIAL_BAD_CTOR_SIGNATURE
diagnostics.message: {kind} function '{name}' must take no parameters and return 'void', but {problem}
diagnostics.cause: Constructor and destructor functions are called by the runtime startup and shutdown sequence, which has nothing to pass to them and nowhere to put a result.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: constructor function.  These are functions that run before control is transferred to the startup function.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_DUPLICATE_PART
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is already a part of this type
diagnostics.cause: Two fields of one product, or two variants of one sum, cannot share a name: the name is how a part is reached, and the specification lets the compiler reorder a product's fields, so there is nothing else to reach one by.  Rename one of them.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: The parts of one type have distinct names.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_CONTAINS_ITSELF
diagnostics.message: '{name}' contains itself, so no value of it would fit in memory
diagnostics.cause: A product holds its fields and a sum holds one of its variants, so a type that reaches itself through either would need room for a value of itself inside a value of itself, without end.  What makes such a shape possible in other languages is indirection -- a pointer, a reference, a box -- and this language has no way to write one yet.  A chain through several definitions counts: the report names the type the chain came back to.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A type may not contain itself.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_FIELD_OF_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is a field of type 'void', which holds nothing
diagnostics.cause: A product holds all of its fields, so one of a type that carries no information is a field that says nothing about a value: the product means exactly what it would mean without it, and the language admits one spelling per meaning.  A *variant* of a sum may be `void`, and says the value is this alternative and carries nothing further -- which is how an enumeration is written.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A field of a product may not be `void`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_REPEATED_TYPE
diagnostics.message: '{type}' is the type of two parts of this sum, so no pattern could tell them apart
diagnostics.cause: An arm of a `match` names the type of the alternative it takes, so two alternatives of one type would be two an arm could not choose between.  This is the rule that makes the patterns work, and it applies to a sum and not to a product: a product holds all of its fields at once and reaches each by name, so two of one type are no trouble there.  Where the two alternatives really are the same type, what tells them apart is a type of their own -- a record of one field named for what it means.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: No two alternatives of a sum have the same type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_NOT_A_CHOICE
diagnostics.message: 'match' takes a sum or a result apart, not '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was written

diagnostics.cause: A `match` exists to say which of several alternatives a value holds, and a type with one alternative has nothing to say.  The two types that have several are a sum, whose alternatives its definition names, and a result, whose two are the answer and the error.  A value of any other type is already the one thing it is.

spec.requirement: `match` applies to a value of a sum or a result type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_UNKNOWN_ALTERNATIVE
diagnostics.message: '{type}' is not one of the alternatives of '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: An arm names the type of the alternative it takes, and this one names a type the value being taken apart has no alternative of -- so the arm could never be the one that runs.  The alternatives are what the definition of the sum lists, or, for a result, its answer type and the error.

spec.requirement: Each arm of a `match` names an alternative of what is taken apart.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_REPEATED_ARM
diagnostics.message: this alternative is already taken by an earlier arm
diagnostics.cause: Two arms taking one alternative means the second can never run: the first takes it.  Where two things should happen for one alternative, they are two statements of one arm.

spec.requirement: No two arms of a `match` take the same alternative.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_NOT_EXHAUSTIVE
diagnostics.message: '{missing}' is an alternative no arm of this 'match' takes
diagnostics.cause: Every alternative must be taken by an arm.  A value holds one of them, and a `match` that left one out would be a program with nowhere to go when the value held it -- which is the thing a sum type exists to make impossible.  There is no catch-all pattern, and that is deliberate: one would let an alternative added later fall silently into a branch written before it existed.

spec.requirement: The arms of a `match` take every alternative.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_BOTTOM_NEEDS_A_RESULT
diagnostics.message: '⊥' takes the error of a result, and this takes '{found}' apart
diagnostics.cause: A sum names its alternatives by their types, so every arm of one is written with a type.  `⊥` exists because a result's two alternatives may name one type -- `u8?u8` is a perfectly good type -- and so cannot both be said by naming one.

spec.requirement: `⊥` is an arm of a result and not of a sum.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_BINDS_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: this alternative carries nothing, so there is no value for '{name}' to be
diagnostics.cause: An arm binds a name to the value the alternative carries.  This one carries none -- its type is `void`, or it is the error of a result whose error carries nothing -- so the name would stand for nothing.  The pattern without the parentheses is how an alternative that carries nothing is taken.

spec.requirement: A pattern binds a name only where the alternative carries a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_ARM_NEVER_RUNS
diagnostics.message: this arm takes nothing an earlier arm left
diagnostics.cause: Every alternative it could take has been taken already, so this arm can never be the one that runs.  A wildcard written after arms that between them take everything is the usual way to reach this, and what it means is that the wildcard is not needed.

spec.requirement: Every arm of a `match` can run.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_DUPLICATE_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is already a value of this enumeration
diagnostics.cause: The names of an enumeration are how its values are written and how an arm of a `match` names one, so two of them alike would be two values nothing could tell apart.

spec.requirement: The values of one enumeration have distinct names.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_HOLDER_TOO_NARROW
diagnostics.message: '{type}' does not hold the value {value} of this enumeration

args.name: value
args.description: a value it does not hold

diagnostics.cause: A definition may say how much room a value of the enumeration takes, and the type it names has to hold every one of the values -- those written down and those the compiler chose.  Leaving the type out lets the compiler choose one that does.

spec.requirement: The type an enumeration names holds every one of its values.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_HOLDER_NOT_INTEGER
diagnostics.message: an enumeration is held in an integer type, not in '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: What the type says is how much room a value takes and how it is aligned, which only an integer type answers here.  It says nothing else: a value of the enumeration is not a number of that type and does not become one.

spec.requirement: The type an enumeration names is an integer type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUM_UNKNOWN_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a value of '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: A value of an enumeration is one of the names its definition lists, written after the name of the type.  This one is not among them.

spec.requirement: A value of an enumeration is one of the names its definition lists.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_WILDCARD_TAKES_NO_NAME
diagnostics.message: '_' takes every alternative left, so there is nothing for a name to be
diagnostics.cause: A pattern that names one alternative binds what that alternative carries.  `_` names every alternative no earlier arm took, and those may carry different things or nothing at all, so there is no one value a name written after it could stand for.

spec.requirement: The wildcard pattern binds no name.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_REPEATED_NUMBER
diagnostics.message: {number} is already the value of '{name}'

args.name: name
args.description: the value that already has it

diagnostics.cause: Two values given one number would be two a program could not tell apart, written as though they were two things.  Where they really are one thing, say so: `second = first` gives the second the value the first has and says outright that the two are one.

spec.requirement: No two values of an enumeration are given the same number outright.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_UNKNOWN_EARLIER_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a value of this enumeration written before this one
diagnostics.cause: A value may be given the number of another by naming it, which says the two are one thing.  The one named has to be a value of the same enumeration and has to be written earlier, since its own number is what this one takes.

spec.requirement: A value named as another's is an earlier value of the same enumeration.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_FLAG_NEEDS_A_REST
diagnostics.message: '{type}' is a flag enumeration, whose values combine, so an arm taking the rest is needed
diagnostics.cause: The values of a flag enumeration are meant to be combined with the bitwise operators, so a value of one may be a combination that no single name stands for.  Naming every one of the names therefore does not account for every value, and `_` is what takes the rest.

spec.requirement: A `match` over a flag enumeration has an arm taking the rest.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_ARM_HAS_NO_VALUE
diagnostics.message: a value is wanted of this 'match', and this arm ends with a statement that has none
diagnostics.cause: Where a value is wanted of a `match`, every arm has to have one, since any of them may be the one that runs.  The statements that have a value are the ones that may be the last of a function's body: an expression, and an assignment, which stands for the variable it changed.  An arm that ends with `return` owes none -- it leaves the function rather than reaching the place the arms join.

spec.requirement: Where a value is wanted of a `match`, every arm produces one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_UNREACHABLE
diagnostics.message: statements after 'return' are never executed
diagnostics.cause: The function returns immediately at the 'return' statement, so the statements that follow it in the same block can never run.  This is usually leftover code, or a 'return' that was meant to be conditional.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_REDUNDANT
diagnostics.message: 'return' can and should be omitted on the last statement of a function
diagnostics.cause: When the value of the last statement is the function's result, the 'return' keyword carries no information and is omitted in the canonical form of the language.  The compiler's own output never writes it.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_MISSING
diagnostics.message: control reaches the end of '{name}' without producing a value of type '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: A function whose return type is not 'void' must produce a value on every path that leaves it.  Because the language admits no undefined behaviour, falling off the end is an error rather than an unspecified result.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_VALUE_IN_VOID
diagnostics.message: returning a value from '{name}', which is declared to return 'void'
diagnostics.cause: The function declares no result, so there is nothing for the returned value to become.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_VALUE_DISCARDED
diagnostics.message: the value of this statement is not used
diagnostics.cause: An expression computes a value and does nothing else, so a statement that is nothing but an expression is a statement with no effect unless something takes the value.  Something does take it in exactly one place: the last statement of a body is the body's result.  Everywhere else the value goes nowhere, and a line that goes nowhere is either a mistake or a leftover -- a generator that emits one has a defect, which is the reason this is an error rather than a warning.  Where the line is meant to stand as it is, `@[ignore(5005)]` on the statement says so.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Statements that are expressions
spec.requirement: A statement that is an expression must have its value used; the last statement of a body is the body's result.

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_ASSIGNMENT_IS_AN_ARROW
diagnostics.message: '=' compares two values; an assignment is written '←'
diagnostics.cause: Attached where the discarded value is a comparison written with '=', which is what someone writes who has spent years in a language where '=' assigns.  The diagnostic itself says the value goes nowhere; this says why the line was probably written.

spec.requirement: An assignment is written `NAME ← VALUE`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED
diagnostics.message: the bootstrap compiler cannot generate code for {construct} yet

args.name: construct
args.description: the construct that has no code generation yet

diagnostics.cause: The bootstrap compiler implements only as much of the language as the compiler's own source needs, so a construct the specification describes may still have no code generation.  This is a limitation of the bootstrap compiler and not an error in the program; the same program will compile once the construct is implemented.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNENCODABLE
diagnostics.message: instruction cannot be encoded: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The instruction, its operands, or the combination of the two cannot be represented in the target's encoding.  From generated code this reports a defect in the compiler; once inline assembly exists it will also report a constraint the written instruction violates, such as naming a high-byte register in a form that carries a REX prefix.

spec.requirement: The backends should use a symbolic version to generate the assembler code to allow, in future, inline assembler code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_UNDEFINED_SYMBOL
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is referenced but never defined
diagnostics.cause: Compilation covers the whole program at once and there is no equivalent of an object file, so every symbol the generated code refers to must be defined by the same compilation.  A symbol that is still undefined at image generation means a function the program calls was never given a body.

spec.requirement: At least for the time being there is only whole-program compilation.  There is no equivalent of object files.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE
diagnostics.message: a value of {value} does not fit the {field} field that must hold it

args.name: value
args.description: the value that does not fit

diagnostics.cause: A displacement, an address or an initial value has to fit the field the instruction or the image reserves for it.  One that does not is reported rather than stored with its upper bits dropped: a program that branched to an address other than the one it named, or started with a value other than the one it was given, would be behaving otherwise than it reads.  A branch too far to reach is the usual cause, and needs a longer form of the instruction, which this compiler does not choose yet.  That a value fits where it is stored is one of the checks the compiler always performs, rather than one it leaves to the reader to have made.

spec.requirement: The compiler predominently has to be fast while at the same time always perform all conformance checks and generating small code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_INTERNAL_ERROR
diagnostics.message: internal compiler error: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The compiler detected an inconsistency in its own data structures, which always indicates a defect in the compiler rather than in the compiled program.  Please report it together with the source that triggered it.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_UNIMPLEMENTED_FEATURE
diagnostics.message: {feature} is not implemented yet

args.name: feature
args.description: the feature the specification describes but the compiler lacks

diagnostics.cause: The specification describes this, and the compiler does not implement it yet.  It reports a gap in the compiler rather than a defect in the program: the same program will compile once the feature exists.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.
